title: Winter fuel payments for 250 households, and what we take to deliver them
story: Silver Birch Relief has run the winter fuel programme in three towns since 2021. Last winter we reached 214 households with a payment of 180 GBP each, paid onto the household's own energy account after a home visit and a means check by two of our caseworkers. This year we are raising 60,000 GBP to reach 250 households on the same model. We take 12.5 percent of what is raised to cover the delivery of the programme: the caseworkers' time, the visits themselves, the annual audit and the bank charges. The remaining 87.5 percent reaches households as the payment. We put the figure on the page because we would rather you weighed it than guessed at it, and our accounts for the last three years are filed and public. Referrals reach us from two food banks, four mosques and the local authority welfare team, and we visit within nine days of a referral. The payment goes onto the energy account rather than as cash because that is what households told us they wanted when we consulted them in 2022; a third of them are on prepayment meters, and a payment onto the account is the version of this that does not vanish into an overdraft before the winter starts. The means check is not paperwork at a distance. A caseworker sits with the household, goes through what comes in and what goes out, writes it on a form the household signs, and we keep those forms for six years so our auditor can sample them. Last winter we turned 31 of the 245 households referred to us down and wrote to each of them saying why. If we do not raise the full amount we will reach fewer households rather than reduce the payment, because 180 GBP was set against the price cap and a smaller payment does not carry a household through a winter. The visits start in the first week of November and the last payments go out before the end of January.

label.notes: The deduction is stated, which is the fact the pipeline is for: published positions among bodies that all consider themselves within the rules run from no deduction at all to a fifth, so the figure is surfaced and the difference is named, and the reviewer is asked which position platform policy applies rather than being handed a verdict on 12.5 percent. The label deliberately does not expect a mixed-use signal here, and that is the judgment this case tests: an administrative deduction is the cost of delivering the one use the money is put to, not a second use it is split between, and a pipeline that reported every stated overhead as a split would fire the wrong question at every competent organisation on the platform. The two need categories stay open because a means check is asserted and no household's position is stated, which is a question the organisation can answer about its own process. The debt line joins them under the sharpened gesture test: the page says a payment onto the energy account is the version of this that does not vanish into an overdraft, which states a fact about what the households it reaches owe, and the organisation can say whether the means check records arrears or an overdrawn account.
